newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Exports drive last Australian c/a def lower.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Exports drive last Australian c/a def lower.

text.p: A strong performance by exports saw Australia's current account deficit narrow by over 25 percent in December, allowing the monthly series to bow out with a flourish.
The current account deficit for December stood at A$1.408 billion, down A$485 million, or 25.6 percent, on November's A$1.893 billion shortfall, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
The release marked the last monthly current account deficit.
From next month, markets will receive a monthly trade and services balance, and current account deficit data on a quarterly basis in the interests of greater accuracy.
"Clearly some of the pessimism about the current account in some quarters has been overstated," Bankers Trust senior economist Peter Munckton said of the December improvement.
Driving the deficit lower in December was a strong 7.9 percent rise in exports, reversing a large fall in November.

"This rebound in exports was spread acoss the rural and non-rural sectors, but the 64 percent increase in cereal exports, mainly wheat, was a standout contributor," Axiom Funds Management chief economist Matthew Drennan said.

The exports performance, after a large fall in November, transformed November's A$384 million trade deficit into a surplus of A$37 million. The trade balance has been in surplus in five of the last seven months.

The December deficit was the last time the monthly current account deficit will be published. The Bureau of Statistics said move was due to the concerns on the accuracy of data on some of the deficit's unreliability of some components.

Data updates on the net income deficit, the largest current account component, were only received quarterly with the monthly figures based on extrapolations of earlier data and were subject to constant and often large revisions.
In future, the current account deficit will be released quarterly and each month there will be a release detailing the balance on international trade in goods and services.
The monthly current account deficit has often been the focus of financial markets' attention, mainly when it was in a deteriorationg phase.

It was during its deterioration in 1986 that it entered the public consciousness when then Treasurer Paul Keating made his famous "banana republic" warning for Australia if the current account contined to worsen.
The demise of the monthly current account data was mourned by few economists, although traders who saw it as a source of market volatility may be more nostalgic.

"I think the real reason I'd like to get the champagne corks out for is the fact that it was the last monthly current account release. It's certainly a release whose passing won't be mourned by many market economists," Nomura economist Andrew Pease said.

Just last year, former Reserve Bank Governor Bernie Fraser said people got too excited about the monthly current account deficit, saying even quarterly and annual data were subject to distortion, and he called for more longer term analysis.

"I know it is a forlorn hope but national stress levels would be lowered dramatically if commentators were more analytical and longer-term in their assessments of current account data," Fraser said in a speech.
It appears he has now got his wish.
